summary: Specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in output feedback mode with the Telnet encryption option, defining two key sizes.

plainLanguage.summary: This picks the CAST-128 scrambler for hiding Telnet text, with a weaker and a stronger key size.

subtitle: Uses CAST-128 encryption in output feedback mode to secure Telnet

tldr.problem: Telnet sends passwords and commands in plain text, exposing them to eavesdropping on insecure networks.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to use the CAST-128 cipher algorithm in 64-bit output feedback mode during Telnet sessions, supporting both 40-bit (weaker) and 128-bit (stronger) key sizes for encryption negotiation.
tldr.outcome: Telnet sessions can negotiate encryption to hide traffic, though output feedback mode does not protect against active attacks or guarantee message integrity.

today: RFC 2949 is a Proposed Standard specifying CAST-128 output feedback mode encryption for Telnet. It remains published but is largely superseded in practice by SSH and other modern secure remote access protocols.

sections.title: Securing Telnet Sessions
sections.content:
Telnet is a protocol for remote terminal access, but it transmits everything—including passwords and commands—in plain text. The Telnet encryption option provides a negotiation mechanism to enable encryption for Telnet sessions.

This RFC specifies how to use the CAST-128 encryption algorithm in 64-bit output feedback mode (OFB64) with the Telnet encryption option. Two key sizes are defined: 40-bit (CAST5_40_OFB64, type 9) and 128-bit (CAST128_OFB64, type 11) encryption keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet normally sends everything you type in plain view. This specifies a scrambler that hides it, with a choice of weak or strong scrambling.

sections.title: Encryption Algorithm
sections.content:
Output feedback mode generates a keystream from the encryption cipher that is then XORed with the plaintext data. Given an 8-byte initial vector, the algorithm produces 8-byte blocks of encrypted output. The process does not require padding and is self-synchronizing when the keystream is lost.

Both parties negotiate an initial vector using the OFB64_IV command. Once an IV_OK response is received, key negotiation proceeds using the ENC_KEYID command. After a common key is identified, START and END commands enable and disable encryption of the session data.
sections.plainLanguage: The cipher creates a random stream of bits that is mixed with the typed text to hide it. Both sides have to agree on the starting seed before the mixing can begin.

sections.title: Security Limitations
sections.content: Output feedback mode does not ensure data integrity. An active attacker may be able to substitute text if he can predict the clear-text that was being transmitted. The 40-bit key mode is explicitly not considered secure and is listed only to document implementations already prevalent on the Internet. Since CPU speeds have increased significantly, the RFC notes that cipher feedback (CFB) mode might be preferable to output feedback mode due to its inherent weaknesses.
sections.plainLanguage: This hides the text from casual listeners, but someone on the network could still trick the connection or guess what you are typing. The 40-bit version is weak and should only be used to work with old systems.

references.text: Adams, C., "The CAST-128 Encryption Algorithm", RFC 2144, May 1997.
